MUQATIL:2:261-262/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:261-262/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:261-262/r1.claim: Spending in God's way means spending in obedience; its reward is likened to a grain producing seven ears with a hundred grains each, and God knows what people spend.

TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r1.claim: The spending passage resumes the loan passage at 2:245 after an intervening account of Israel, the challenger of Abraham, the ruined town, and Abraham’s question about resurrection.

TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r2.claim: The inserted narratives argue for resurrection against polytheists and urge believers to fight, promising divine aid despite being outnumbered and defeat for the enemy.

TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r3.claim: The narratives also expose concealed Jewish affairs to establish Muhammad’s revelation, and warn hypocrites that divine punishment may reach them as it did earlier people.

TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r4.claim: The grain image compares spending one’s own wealth in jihad with a seed bearing seven ears, each with a hundred grains: a seven-hundredfold reward.

TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p650#2/r5.claim: The seed may be wheat, barley, or another crop that produces ears when sown.

TAB-FULL:v4p652/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r1.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r1.claim: Al-Suddi says one who spends in God’s cause receives seven hundredfold reward.

TAB-FULL:v4p652/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd says the parable concerns spending on oneself while going out in God’s cause.

TAB-FULL:v4p652/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r3.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r3.claim: Al-Rabi distinguishes seven-hundredfold reward for those pledged to migrate and stationed in Medina from tenfold for those pledged only to Islam.

TAB-FULL:v4p652/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r4.claim: If a grain can bear one hundred seeds in each of seven ears, the image is literal; otherwise it can mean a seed produces seven ears with one hundred seeds each.

TAB-FULL:v4p652/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r5.claim: A further possible reading attributes the hundred seeds to the original grain because they grew from it.

TAB-FULL:v4p652/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r6.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p652/r6.claim: Al-Dahhak says each ear itself grows one hundred seeds, representing the reward for spending in God’s cause.

TAB-FULL:v4p653/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p653/r1.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p653/r1.claim: One interpretation gives the seven-hundredfold multiplication specifically to spending in God’s cause, while denying that added promise to other spending.

TAB-FULL:v4p653/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p653/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p653/r2.claim: A second view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas says God may multiply a spender’s reward beyond seven hundred to two millionfold; al-Tabari omits it because its chain was unavailable.

TAB-FULL:v4p653/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p653/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p653/r3.claim: Al-Tabari prefers that God multiplies the seven hundred as much as He wills for those spending in His cause, since the passage mentions no other spending.

ZAJJAJ:v1p346/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p346/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p346/r4.claim: After establishing proof of oneness and prophetic signs, God urges struggle against disbelief; spending and striving for truth earn great reward, with a seven-hundredfold multiplication.

ZAJJAJ:v1p346/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p346/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p346/r5.claim: God’s generosity is unlimited, and He knows where to place His gift.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r1.speaker: مكحول
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r1.claim: Makhul interprets spending in God's path as tethered horses prepared for service in God's cause.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r2.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr glosses “in God's path” as “in obedience to God.”

IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r3.speaker: ابن عمر
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r3.claim: Ibn Umar says that after hearing of the seven-hundredfold reward, the Prophet asked for more for his community; God then revealed 2:245, and after another request, 39:10.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r4.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r4.claim: Ikrima calculates the parable's yield as seven hundred grains per seed.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r5.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r5.claim: Al-Suddi says this seven-hundredfold reward is for whoever spends in God's path.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r6.speaker: الربيع
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r6.claim: Al-Rabi says those in Medina who pledged to the Prophet and only went on expeditions with his permission received seven hundredfold for a good deed, while pledging to Islam brought tenfold.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p514/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says pilgrimage spending and jihad spending are equal: each dirham receives seven hundredfold because both are in God's path.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p515/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p515/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p515/r1.claim: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that God multiplies a good deed two thousandfold.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p515/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p515/r2.speaker: النبي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p515/r2.claim: The Prophet says a person who funds an expedition while staying home receives seven hundredfold for each dirham, while one who goes and spends on the campaign receives seven hundred thousandfold; he recites this verse.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p515/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p515/r3.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNABIHATIM:v2p515/r3.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr explains “knowing” as knowing what will happen.

THALABI:v2p257#2/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p257#2/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p257#2/r1.claim: The verse's compressed comparison means the likeness of the charity of those who spend in God's path; alternatively, it compares the spenders themselves to a farmer sowing a seed.

THALABI:v2p257#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p257#2/r2.speaker: أبو عمرو وأبو غزية وحمزة والكسائي
THALABI:v2p257#2/r2.claim: These readers assimilate the tāʾ in sanābil to the following sīn; others pronounce the two words distinctly, the common language.

THALABI:v2p257#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p257#2/r3.speaker: أبو عمرو
THALABI:v2p257#2/r3.claim: Abū ʿAmr cites a line that turns sīn into tāʾ, with al-nāt intended to mean al-nās, as evidence for assimilation.

THALABI:v2p257#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p257#2/r4.speaker: أبو جعفر والأعمش
THALABI:v2p257#2/r4.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and al-Aʿmash shorten the readings of khams miʾah and miʾah; the other readers lengthen them.

THALABI:v2p257#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p257#2/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p257#2/r5.claim: Thaʿlabī says a spike with a hundred grains is not impossible; if none is observed, the comparison can mean one planted seed produces seven spikes of a hundred grains apiece.

THALABI:v2p257#2/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p257#2/r6.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v2p257#2/r6.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says that every spike produced a hundred grains.

THALABI:v2p257#2/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p257#2/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p257#2/r7.claim: God may multiply the reward from seven to seventy or seven hundred and beyond, to an amount known only to God.

THALABI:v2p258/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p258/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p258/r1.claim: God is ample in the reward multiples and knows who spends.

THALABI:v2p258/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p258/r2.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v2p258/r2.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says a person who gives one dirham seeking God's pleasure receives seven hundred dirhams in immediate worldly replacement and meets a thousand on Judgment Day.

THALABI:v2p258/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p258/r3.speaker: الكلبي
THALABI:v2p258/r3.claim: Al-Kalbī says the verse was revealed about ʿUthmān and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf: the latter gave four thousand dirhams and kept four thousand for his family; the Prophet blessed both parts.

THALABI:v2p258/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p258/r4.speaker: الكلبي
THALABI:v2p258/r4.claim: The same occasion report says ʿUthmān equipped a thousand camels for the Tabūk expedition and donated the well of Rumah to Muslims.

THALABI:v2p258/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p258/r5.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن سمرة
THALABI:v2p258/r5.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samura reports that ʿUthmān brought a thousand dinars for the army of hardship, and the Prophet praised what he had done.

THALABI:v2p258/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p258/r6.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
THALABI:v2p258/r6.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī says he saw the Prophet pray for ʿUthmān until dawn, after which the verse was revealed about him.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r1.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r1.claim: Ibn Zayd says spending in God's way means spending in jihad; another view includes every kind of good work.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r2.claim: The grain's seven ears, each holding a hundred grains, picture a seven-hundredfold reward for spending in God's way.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd says other acts of obedience receive tenfold reward, while al-Dahhak says they may also be multiplied seven hundredfold.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r4.claim: God's multiplying may mean multiplying this stated reward for whomever He wills or increasing it beyond that amount.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r5.speaker: ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p336/r5.claim: The All-Encompassing is not constrained from increasing reward and knows who deserves it; another explanation is vast mercy and knowledge of the spending, or unlimited power and knowledge of what is beneficial.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r1.speaker: أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r1.claim: This parable continues 2:245; the intervening verses are a parenthetical summons to truth through arguments and signs.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r2.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r2.claim: After proving unity and recounting the messengers' proofs, God urges jihad and promises great reward for fighting and spending; good deeds earn tenfold, while jihad spending can be multiplied seven hundredfold.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r3.claim: The construction means the likeness of spenders' charity or spending, or the likeness of people spending like a sower; it omits an understood noun.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r4.claim: The hundred-grain ear need only be imaginable for the analogy; some say millet can produce it, while another explanation is that one grain sown yields a hundred.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p407/r5.claim: God multiplies reward for whomever He wills; واسع means generous and not diminished by bestowing bounty, and عليم knows who spends.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:261-263/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:261-263/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:261-263/r1.claim: The seed parable represents charitable spending: one gift may be multiplied seven hundredfold, but this is a simile and does not require that such a crop literally exist.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r1.claim: The comparison means the reward of the spenders' charity, like a seed sown by a farmer, and 'God's path' may mean jihad or every kind of good.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r2.speaker: الضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r2.claim: Al-Dahhak explains the hundred grains as what each planted grain produces, not necessarily a single visible head already holding a hundred grains.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r3.claim: A hundredfold head is possible even if not commonly seen; a conceivable, non-impossible case can serve as a parable.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r4.claim: God may multiply the seven-hundredfold return further, from seven to seventy, seven hundred, or whatever measure He wills beyond human knowledge.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p324#2/r5.claim: Wasi means wealthy and giving abundantly; alim means knowing the intention of the person who spends.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338#2/r1.claim: God multiplies the reward for whoever He wills, not every giver, because givers' circumstances differ; alternatively, He may increase the seven hundredfold further for those who merit it.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r1.claim: The parable omits a genitive: either the givers' expenditure is like a seed, or the givers are like someone sowing a seed; God truly causes growth, though it is attributed to seed, earth, or water as causes.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r2.claim: One grain grows a stalk with seven branches and an ear on each; the image makes multiplied reward visible to the observer.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r3.claim: The image is found in millet and sorghum, and wheat stalks can sometimes branch to that yield in fertile fields; even if unattested, a hypothetical image is valid.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p338/r4.claim: The plural سنابل rather than the expected paucity form سنبلات is acceptable because plural patterns can substitute for one another, as discussed for qurūʾ.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r1.claim: The verse presents spending in God’s cause as a noble example and urges it; it concerns voluntary spending, and God’s cause includes all obedient acts benefiting Muslims and the community, especially jihad.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r10.claim: Sunbula derives from the crop’s sending out its contents and has the plural sanābil.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r11.claim: The syntax elides a possessive: the likeness is of the spending of those who give, or of the owner of a grain; al-Ṭabarī takes the hundred grains as conditional on finding such an ear.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r12.speaker: الضحاك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r12.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk glosses “a hundred grains in each ear” as each ear producing a hundred grains; al-Ṭabarī treats this as equivalent to his own reading, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya says that is not required by al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s wording.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r13.speaker: بعضهم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r13.claim: Some readers place the accusative on “a hundred grains,” construing it as the object of “it produced.”

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r2.claim: Grain is a generic term for what people cultivate and eat, especially wheat; al-Mutalammis’s poem illustrates the word.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r3.speaker: المتلمس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r3.claim: Al-Mutalammis uses ḥabb to mean grain, eaten by weevils in the village.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r4.claim: A wheat ear can contain a hundred grains, though other crops may produce more; the example simply uses this figure.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r5.claim: Other Qur’anic passages promise tenfold reward for good deeds; spending in jihad earns seven hundredfold, as a sound report explains.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r6.speaker: طائفة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r6.claim: One group takes “God multiplies for whom He wills” to restate and reinforce the seven hundredfold, with no increase beyond it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r7.speaker: طائفة من العلماء
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r7.claim: Another group says God may multiply the reward beyond seven hundredfold.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r8.claim: A report attributes to Ibn ʿAbbās a multiplication up to two million, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya says its chain is not established.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r9.speaker: ابن عمر
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p355#2/r9.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports that when this verse came down, the Prophet asked for more reward for his community; 57:11 and then 39:10 followed, after he asked again.

TABRISI:2:261/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:261/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:261/r1.claim: Nabat refers to plants or vegetation; anbata is to make something grow, and related forms name adolescence, the poppy tree, and other growth.

TABRISI:2:261/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:261/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:261/r2.claim: Sunbula follows a pattern related to sending something down; a grain-bearing ear is so called because its contents are covered like a hanging curtain.

TABRISI:2:261/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:261/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:261/r3.claim: The parable can compare charitable spending with a grain, or compare the spenders with a sower; سبيل الله includes jihad and all forms of righteousness in the general view transmitted from Abu Abd Allah and chosen by Abu Ali al-Jubba'i.

TABRISI:2:261/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:261/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:261/r4.claim: A narrower view restricts spending in God's path here to jihad; on that view other devotional acts receive tenfold reward rather than this multiplication.

TABRISI:2:261/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:261/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:261/r5.claim: The image promises seven hundredfold reward, with God able to multiply even further or to grant this increase to whomever he wills.

TABRISI:2:261/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:261/r6.speaker: محمد
TABRISI:2:261/r6.claim: Ibn Umar reports that after this verse the Prophet prayed for a greater increase for his community; verses promising abundant multiplication and uncounted reward followed.

TABRISI:2:261/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:261/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:261/r7.claim: The hypothetical yield of a hundred grains is possible even if unseen, as with imagined creatures in poetry and the Qur'anic image of devils' heads; millet supplies an actual example.

TABRISI:2:261/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:261/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:261/r8.claim: Wide capacity means either power or mercy; Ali ibn Zayd explains all-knowing as knowing who deserves added reward or what intention motivates the spending.

TABRISI:2:261/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:261/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:261/r9.claim: The verse connects to the invitation in 2:245; the intervening material is an exhortation and presentation of proofs, or the command to fight and finance those who reject the proofs, according to al-Zajjaj.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r1.speaker: ثعلب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r1.claim: The parable concerns the charitable expenditure, not the men; Arabic omits a word like “example” when context makes it clear.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r2.speaker: ثعلب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r2.claim: This ellipsis resembles “they were made to drink the calf into their hearts,” where love is understood, and the description of misers in 3:18, where miserliness is supplied.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r3.claim: “In God's path” may mean jihad or all forms of goodness.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r4.speaker: أبو سليمان الدمشقي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r4.claim: The verse connects to the earlier command to believers to spend from what God provided.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r5.claim: The parable teaches that a good deed spent in God's path is multiplied seven hundredfold.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r6.speaker: الشعبي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r6.claim: A man's spending on himself and his household is multiplied seven hundredfold.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r7.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p316/r7.claim: God's multiplying for whom He wills means increasing the reward beyond seven hundredfold.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r1.speaker: القفال
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r1.claim: Al-Qaffal says the parable works even if no real ear has one hundred grains: anyone seeking worldly profit would plant one grain for a seven-hundredfold return, and the same logic should motivate afterlife reward.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r2.claim: The alternative claim that such a spikelet was seen in millet is extremely weak.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r3.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r3.claim: Abu Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i assimilate the t in أنبتت with the s in سبع because both letters are voiceless; the others pronounce both distinctly.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r4.claim: The verse does not specify the amount of God's multiplication or who receives it; it may encompass all the pious or distinguish some for greater sincerity or divine acceptance.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p39#2/r5.claim: God is vast in power to reward generously according to the amount and kind of spending, so no worker's deed is lost.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r1.claim: After establishing knowledge of God and resurrection, the passage turns to laws and obligations, beginning with the duties involved in spending wealth.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r2.speaker: القاضي
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r2.claim: Al-Qadi sees 2:261 as explaining the abundant multiplication promised in 2:245; the resurrection proofs in between establish why spending is not futile, since God rewards a single seed with seven hundred grains.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r3.speaker: الأصم
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r3.claim: Al-Asamm says the seed parable follows the proof of the Prophet to encourage giving wealth and risking oneself to support him and establish his law.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r4.claim: Another proposed connection contrasts the believer's spending in God's way with the unbeliever's spending in the way of false patrons, following the preceding contrast in guardianship.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r5.claim: The omitted comparison is either the likeness of the spenders' donations to a seed or the likeness of a farmer planting a seed.

RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p39/r6.claim: Spending in God's way means spending for His religion: some limit it to jihad, while others include all good, obligatory and voluntary spending for migration, jihad, charity, and public benefit.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r1.claim: Some say the verse concerned voluntary charity or was abrogated by the zakāt verse; the author says abrogation need not be claimed because spending in God’s cause remains recommended at all times.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r2.claim: God’s paths are numerous, with jihad the greatest because it raises God’s word above all others.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r3.claim: Ḥabba is a generic name for what people grow and eat, especially wheat; the word has other senses including a seed of the heart, a legume seed, love, or a beloved person, while sunbula names a grain-bearing ear.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r4.claim: Some identify the ears as millet, but the author rejects this because millet ears carry far more than one hundred grains; wheat can reach one hundred, and other grains may exceed that, so the verse gives an illustrative number.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r5.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r5.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reads “a hundred grains in each ear” as a hypothetical case if that yield occurs; he also quotes al-Ḍaḥḥāk saying each ear in the parable produces a hundred.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r6.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says al-Ṭabarī wrongly treats al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s statement as equivalent to a mere supposition; the two views do not entail one another.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r7.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني ويعقوب الحضرمي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#2/r7.claim: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī and Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī report an accusative reading of “a hundred” that supplies the verb “it produced.”

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r1.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r1.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī assimilate the tāʾ into the sīn in “it produced seven ears,” since both sounds are voiceless; the rest retain the unassimilated form.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r2.speaker: أبو عمرو
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r2.claim: Abū ʿAmr cites a poetic line saying “al-nāt” for “al-nās,” demonstrating interchange of tāʾ and sīn.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r3.claim: The Qurʾān gives a tenfold reward for good deeds generally, while this verse specifies seven hundredfold for charity in jihad.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r4.speaker: طائفة من العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r4.claim: One group reads “God multiplies for whom He wills” as reaffirming the seven hundredfold figure, with no increase beyond it.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r5.claim: The author prefers the view that God may multiply beyond seven hundred, supported by the Ibn ʿUmar report mentioned earlier.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r6.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r6.claim: A report from ʿAlī, Abū al-Dardāʾ, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Umāma, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, Jābir, and ʿImrān says a person who funds jihad from home receives seven hundred per dirham, while one who fights and spends receives seven hundred thousand.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#3/r7.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says multiplication may reach two million; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says its chain is not sound.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r1.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r1.claim: The Prophet says a Muslim who plants or sows and from it a bird, person, or animal eats receives charity’s reward.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r2.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r2.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports the Prophet’s instruction to seek provision in the hidden places of the earth, meaning through cultivation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r3.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r3.claim: The Prophet praises date palms as firmly rooted in mud and feeding people during famine; the author says this is praise of the palm.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r4.claim: Agriculture and tree planting are communal obligations, and the ruler must compel people to maintain them.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r5.speaker: ابن شهاب الزهري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r5.claim: Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī’s poem urges ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Malik to cultivate hidden parts of the land and pray for rain, promising lasting wealth even when water recedes.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r6.speaker: المعتضد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261#4/r6.claim: A report says the caliph al-Muʿtaḍid dreamed that ʿAlī handed him a hoe and called it the keys to the earth’s treasures.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r1.claim: After presenting proofs of resurrection, God urges jihad and promises a great reward to those who fight after such prophetic proof.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r2.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet asked God to increase the reward for his community; verses promising multiplied loans and uncapped patience rewards followed.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r3.claim: The verse illustrates the nobility and goodness of spending in God’s cause and urges it; its fuller comparison is spending as seed, like a farmer planting a grain that grows seven ears of a hundred grains each.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r4.claim: The sower represents the giver and the seed represents charity: God gives seven hundred good deeds per gift, with still greater yield for a righteous giver who gives good wealth in its proper place.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r5.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن عوف وعثمان
QURTUBI-FULL:2:261/r5.claim: A report says the verse concerned ʿUthmān and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf’s gifts for the Tabūk expedition: Ibn ʿAwf donated half his eight thousand, while ʿUthmān equipped those lacking provisions.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r1.claim: The comparison means either that the donors' spending resembles a seed or that the donors resemble a person sowing one, with an omitted noun.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r2.claim: The seed is credited with sprouting because it is a cause, as earth and water are; God is the true grower, who brings seven branches, each bearing a hundred-grain ear.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r3.claim: This is an illustrative parable, not a claim that such growth must actually occur; it may occur in millet or, in fertile land, wheat.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r4.claim: God multiplies reward according to His favor and the donor's sincerity and effort, explaining why deeds receive different measures of reward.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:261/r5.claim: God's bounty is ample and unconfined, and He knows the donor's intention and the amount given.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r1.claim: After demonstrating God's power to revive, the passage urges spending in God's path and promises a great reward that He is able to grant.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r2.claim: The comparison omits a possessive: it means the likeness of their expenditure, or the likeness of a sower who plants a seed.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r3.claim: God is the true grower, but the seed is credited with growing because it is the cause; one stem branches into seven ears of a hundred grains each.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r4.claim: The image makes multiplied rewards visible; millet and sorghum exemplify it, and wheat can sometimes branch to this yield in fertile soil; the parable also works hypothetically.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r5.claim: Sanābil replaces the expected plural sunbulāt just as qurūʾ replaces aqrāʾ.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r6.claim: God does not multiply seven hundredfold for every spender because conditions differ, or He may increase beyond seven hundred for whom He wills.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r7.speaker: الشامي
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r7.claim: The Shami reading has yudaʿʿifu; the Makki reading has yuḍāʿifu.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p128/r8.claim: God is abundant in grace and generosity and knows spenders' intentions.

QASHANI:2:261-262/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:261-262/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:261-262/r1.claim: The first kind of spending is in the realm of action, given in hope of God's reward; its return begins at seven hundredfold and may grow without limit by divine will.

QASHANI:2:261-262/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:261-262/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:261-262/r2.claim: God's giving exceeds human giving without measure, and He knows donors' intentions and belief that the gift comes from His bounty.

QASHANI:2:261-262/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:261-262/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:261-262/r3.claim: The second kind is giving from witnessing divine attributes for God's pleasure rather than His gift; the third is giving through God from witnessing the Essence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649#2/r1.claim: حبة is a generic name for cultivated, edible seed, especially wheat; the poet al-Mutalammis uses حب for grain eaten by a grain beetle. Other forms mean heart’s dark center, vegetable seed, grain, or beloved.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649#2/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649#2/r2.claim: الإنبات means bringing something forth by growth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p649#2/r3.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says سنبلة is usually analyzed as فنعلة, with nūn augmentative; some linguists attest سنبل, while his colleagues disagree over whether nūn is original.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r7.claim: After the resurrection demonstrations in the passerby and Abraham stories, the passage turns to spending whose benefit will appear at resurrection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p652/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p652/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p652/r1.claim: The spending passage echoes قرضا حسنا after the Israelites’ death-avoidance story and انفقوا before the Day after David and Goliath; charity presupposes resurrection-belief, and the seed’s seven hundredfold growth demonstrates power to revive the dead.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p652/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p652/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p652/r2.claim: Another coherence reading moves from creation and return to legal duties, beginning with spending and then turning to lawful acquisition; the verse elaborates earlier general commands to spend and supports their reliance on resurrection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p652/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p652/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p652/r3.claim: Here مثل means description; the comparison may omit “the spender” or “the grower,” or omit both with different implied subjects, as in the earlier disbeliever-and-caller parable.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r1.claim: The parable urges spending on every obedience that benefits Muslims, especially jihad; although some restrict سبيل الله here to jihad, its apparent scope includes required or voluntary spending for oneself or others to support worship.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r2.claim: Spending is likened to cultivation because a planted crop keeps reproducing.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r3.claim: The Ḥijāzī readers, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn Dhakwān pronounce the feminine تاء in أنبتت before س; the other readers assimilate it, facilitated by the sounds’ proximity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r4.claim: The seed is credited with growing metaphorically as its cause, though God is the actual grower; one stalk branches into seven, each bearing a hundred grains, picturing the multiplied reward vividly.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the seven hundred grains can occur in millet and maize, possibly in productive wheat, and the parable remains valid as a supposition even if unseen.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r6.speaker: ابن عيسى
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r6.claim: Ibn ʿĪsā says the example occurs in millet, while parables may also use what can be imagined without being observed; he supports this with poetic comparisons to mythical ogres.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r7.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p653/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says a wheat head may have one hundred grains and other grains more; the chosen figure illustrates jihad spending’s seven-hundredfold reward, beside the general tenfold reward for good works and a sound hadith.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p654/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p654/r1.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p654/r1.claim: Seven is preferred as a culturally salient high number: seven, seventy, and seven hundred recur in Arabic and scripture, while reports describe reward expanding through seven hundred, seven thousand, and beyond counting.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p654/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p654/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p654/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī asks why this verse uses the plural سنابل instead of the sound feminine سنبلات as in Joseph, and answers that plural forms may substitute for one another.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p654/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p654/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p654/r3.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects Zamakhsharī’s unrestricted substitution rule: sound plurals mark three to ten only when no other plural exists or when parallel wording favors them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r1.claim: A rare reading puts مائة حبة in the accusative, explained by an omitted “produced”; parsing it as a badal fails under the normal categories unless one also supplies omitted حب.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r2.claim: مائة may mean the ordinary number or simply abundant grain, since Arabs use one hundred hyperbolically.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r3.claim: The example presents farming as one of people’s highest occupations; a sound Muslim report counts crops eaten by humans, animals, or birds as charity, and another report adds what is lost.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r4.claim: A report in al-Tirmidhī urges seeking provision in the hidden places of the earth, interpreted here as farming; a cited poem likewise asks God to bless cultivation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r5.claim: Agriculture is a collective duty; if everyone agrees to abandon it, some people may be compelled to perform it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r6.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656#2/r6.claim: Some say multiplication stops at seven hundred; others say God may multiply beyond that.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656/r1.claim: When a word has a sound plural and a broken plural, an established broken plural of abundance, especially on مفاعل, is preferred for counts three to ten; sound plurals are limited or rare according to the other plural’s pattern and usage.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p656/r2.claim: في كل سنبلة may modify سنابل in the genitive or سبع in the accusative; مائة is best parsed as the subject licensed by the preposition, and سنبلة منها is understood.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r1.claim: A report attributes multiplication up to two million to Ibn ʿAbbās, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya says its chain is not sound; al-Ḍaḥḥāk says it reaches thousands upon thousands.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r2.claim: A report from Ibn ʿUmar says that after this parable was revealed, the Prophet prayed for more reward for his community, then the verse promising patient people reward without measure was revealed; the al-Nasāʾī version also places قرضا حسنا between them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r3.claim: لمن يشاء means God multiplies for whom He wills, with an omitted qualification tied to His will; Zamakhsharī says multiplication varies by spenders’ states or exceeds seven hundred for those who merit it, and Abū Ḥayyān flags “merit” as Muʿtazilite insinuation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p657/r4.claim: واسع means abundant in giving and عليم means knowing the intention; another explanation makes God vast in power to recompense and knowledgeable of each expenditure’s measure and reward.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r3.speaker: عاصم الجحدري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p667/r3.claim: He reads حبة with ḥāʾ; the author says بربوة is locative, an adjectival phrase attached to an omitted noun.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r1.claim: Anbatat sabʿa sanābil is an adjectival clause describing ḥabbah as a grain that sprouted seven ears.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r2.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Hishām assimilate the feminine tāʾ into the sīn of sabʿ; the others pronounce it distinctly. Near articulation and analogical alternations such as nās/nāt explain the assimilation, witnessed in verse.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī asks why this verse uses the broken plural sanābil rather than the sound plural sanbilāt as in Q 12:43, and says plural patterns interchange by extension; the author finds this answer inadequate.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r4.claim: Sound plurals quantify numbers only when no other plural exists, as with samāwāt, baqarāt, āyāt, and ṣalawāt; the rare poetic samāyā is disregarded. They can also be chosen through adjacency, as sanbilāt beside baqarāt in Q 12:43.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r5.claim: Without adjacency, when a noun has both sound and broken plurals the broken plural is used for counting; sound forms such as ṭarīqāt and laylāt are possible but disfavored beside seven paths or nights.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#2/r6.claim: Among competing plurals, mafaʿil broken plurals are preferred to sound plurals (e.g. three Aḥmads/Zaynabs); when the non-sound plural is uncommon, sound or common broken forms are preferred, with the rare alternatives noted.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r1.claim: Sunbulah has two analyses: nūn is original because sunbala al-zarʿ means the crop produced its ear, or nūn is extra (the common view) because asbala al-zarʿ is attested; the two verb patterns resemble sabaṭ/sabaṭr.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r2.claim: Fī kulli sunbula is an adjectival phrase modifying sanābil (genitive) or sabʿ (accusative), in either case dependent on an omitted term; miʾah can be the prepositional phrase's subject or a fronted predicate with miʾah as subject.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r3.claim: The first parse of marfūʿ miʾah, as the subject licensed by the dependent prepositional phrase, is preferable because single-word modifiers are the default; an omitted pronoun means 'in each ear of them'.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r4.claim: The majority raise miʾah; a reading accusative is possible by an omitted verb ('it produced/brought forth') or as badal of sabʿ, but the author rejects the proposed whole, part, and inclusion appositions because their relations fail.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261#3/r5.claim: The simplest account of accusative miʾah deletes a noun: 'the grain of seven ears'; then miʾata ḥabbah is a partitive apposition to that omitted grain.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261/r1.claim: Mathal is the subject and ka-mathali ḥabbah its predicate; the comparison requires an ellipsis because spenders are not themselves like a grain. Proposed omissions are the spender/their spending, the sower of a grain, or matching omissions on both sides.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261/r2.claim: The author refers readers to his fuller analysis of Q 2:171; treating either kāf or mathal as an extra word is very remote and should be disregarded.

SAMIN-DURR:2:261/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:261/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:261/r3.claim: Ḥabbah is one edible grain, most often wheat; al-Mutalammis supplies poetic evidence. With kasrah, ḥibbah means vegetable seeds not eaten as staple, while ḥubb with ḍamma means grain.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r1.claim: Muslim's wording has a man bring a branded camel as a gift for God's cause, and the Prophet promises seven hundred camels in return.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r2.claim: The Prophet says good deeds are multiplied tenfold to seven hundred except fasting, which belongs to God and He rewards; the fasting person has two joys and a scent more pleasing than musk.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r3.claim: The Prophet says deeds are multiplied tenfold up to seven hundred or more, except fasting, which is for God; the fasting person leaves food and desire for Him, enjoys breaking the fast and meeting Him, and has a scent dearer to God than musk. Fasting is a shield.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r4.speaker: خريم بن فاتك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r4.claim: The Prophet said spending in God's cause is multiplied seven hundredfold.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r5.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r5.claim: A report says prayer, fasting, and remembrance receive a seven-hundredfold multiplier in relation to spending in God's cause.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r6.speaker: عمران بن حصين
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691#2/r6.claim: A strange report says a person who funds an expedition while staying home receives seven hundred per dirham, while one who goes out and spends receives seven hundred thousand per dirham; the Prophet then recited this verse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r1.claim: The seed parable depicts God multiplying charity spent in His cause for His pleasure, from tenfold to seven hundredfold.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r2.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr interprets spending in God's cause as spending in obedience to Him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r3.speaker: مكحول
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r3.claim: Makḥūl interprets it as military spending, including keeping horses ready, preparing weapons, and similar costs.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, through Shabīb ibn Bishr and ʿIkrima, applies it to jihad and pilgrimage, where a dirham can be multiplied seven hundredfold.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r5.claim: The growing-seed image affects people more strongly than simply naming seven hundred because God nurtures good deeds like crops in fertile ground.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r6.speaker: أبو عبيدة بن الجراح
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r6.claim: The Prophet said surplus spending in God's cause earns seven hundredfold, while spending on oneself or family, visiting a sick person, or removing harm earns tenfold; fasting is a shield unless broken, and bodily affliction erases sins. A report is partly transmitted by al-Nasāʾī, including a mawqūf version.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r7.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p691/r7.claim: The Prophet said that whoever gives a branded she-camel in God's cause will receive seven hundred branded camels at the Resurrection.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r1.claim: A report previously cited at 2:245 says a good deed may be multiplied to two million good deeds.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r2.claim: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet asked God to increase his community's reward; 2:245 followed, then after another request 39:10 came down. Ibn Ḥibbān also transmits the report in his Ṣaḥīḥ.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r3.claim: God's multiplication varies according to the spender's sincerity.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p692/r4.claim: God is vast in abundant bounty and knows who deserves it and who does not.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p514/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p514/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p514/r1.claim: After Abraham's birds, the passage turns to spending before the Day when only divinely prescribed means can help; it renews the surah's opening call to the God-fearing and recalls the command to spend.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p514/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p514/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p514/r2.claim: The seed parable makes the promised multiplication explicit and includes the general command to spend; its plant growth also offers ordinary people a perceptible analogy for resurrection after Abraham's extraordinary sign.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p514/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p514/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p514/r3.claim: The transition contrasts Abraham's exceptional bird revival, granted to a firmly believing person, with ordinary plant growth that can reveal resurrection to anyone who reflects.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r1.claim: Spending wealth in God's cause is compared with a sower's grain; grain is the most complete food, while fruit serves as a relish.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r2.claim: Ḥabb denotes fully ripened vegetation fit to nourish humans, the most complete creatures; grain is more complete as food, while fruit is more complete as accompaniment.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r3.claim: The seed produces seven ears through God's created power, aided by good soil and balanced watering; each ear gathers its grain in a sheath.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r4.claim: The ear's gathered grain signifies people who share a provision and cooperate in their affairs; grain is gathered, not solitary.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r5.claim: Seven signifies completion and multiplication: Arabs use seven to express abundance above or below its literal count, making seven hundred the minimum promised return before limitless increase.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r6.claim: The parable uses ellipsis by correspondence: it states the spender first, implying the omitted sower later, and states the grain later, implying the omitted expenditure first.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r7.claim: God increases reward for whomever He wills, with power unconstrained by any attribute and knowledge of spenders' intentions determining their measure of reward.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r8.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r8.claim: The closing names Vast and Knowing frame the whole parable section: God's encompassing power makes reward fitting in both worlds, and His knowledge misses no deed.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r9.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p515/r9.claim: Just as weather can reduce or destroy a crop, factors arising after a donation can diminish or void its reward, so the text warns against what invalidates spending.

DURR-FULL:v2p36/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says the parable’s grain yields a seven-hundredfold reward.

DURR-FULL:v2p36/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r5.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r5.claim: Al-Suddī says one who spends in God’s path receives seven hundred times the reward.

DURR-FULL:v2p36/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r6.speaker: ابن زيد
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r6.claim: Ibn Zayd says God is vast in generosity and knows whom to increase.

DURR-FULL:v2p36/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r7.speaker: الربيع
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r7.claim: Al-Rabīʿ says a person who pledged allegiance to migrate, stayed with the Prophet in Medina, and campaigned only with his permission received seven hundredfold; allegiance to Islam alone brought tenfold.

DURR-FULL:v2p36/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r8.speaker: عمران بن حصين
DURR-FULL:v2p36/r8.claim: A report from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn says sending an expense for God’s path while remaining home earns seven hundredfold, while personally campaigning and spending earns seven hundred thousandfold per dirham on Judgment Day.

DURR-FULL:v2p39/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p39/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p39/r1.claim: Spending for pilgrimage and jihad alike earns seven hundredfold because both are for God's cause.

DURR-FULL:v2p39/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p39/r2.speaker: بريدة
DURR-FULL:v2p39/r2.claim: The Prophet likens spending on pilgrimage to spending in God's cause: one dirham earns seven hundredfold.

DURR-FULL:v2p39/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p39/r3.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v2p39/r3.claim: Anas reports the same seven-hundredfold reward for spending on pilgrimage as for God's cause.

DURR-FULL:v2p39/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p39/r4.speaker: معاذ بن أنس
DURR-FULL:v2p39/r4.claim: The Prophet says prayer, fasting, and remembrance are multiplied seven hundredfold beyond spending in God's cause.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p341/r1.claim: The parable compares the expenditure, not the people themselves, to a seed, since a human being is not like an inanimate plant.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r10.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p341/r10.claim: A prophetic parable depicts generosity as a tree rooted in Paradise and miserliness as one rooted in Hell, each drawing followers toward its destination.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r11.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r11.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p341/r11.claim: Earning support for a widow and a poor person is likened to jihad because caring for them demands patience and struggle against the self.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p341/r2.claim: Spending in God's path covers both obligatory and voluntary forms of charitable good; a seed planted in fertile land yields seven stalks, each with a hundred grains.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p341/r3.claim: The seven-hundredfold crop is observable in productive land and may be exceeded by some grains.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p341/r4.claim: God may multiply the reward further according to His will and the giver's sincerity and effort, which explains why rewards differ.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p341/r5.claim: God's abundance is unrestricted, and He knows the giver's intention, amount, and how the money was earned.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p341/r6.claim: Like a skilled farmer with good seed and fertile soil, a righteous giver with wholesome wealth who places it properly receives greater growth.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r7.speaker: أبو هريرة
BURSEVI:v1p341/r7.claim: Abu Hurayra transmits the Prophet's teaching that God accepts only wholesome earnings and grows even a single date of charity until it is mountain-sized.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p341/r8.claim: The Prophet's image of God nurturing a charitable gift signals that charity needs this special cultivation because love of wealth tends to diminish its quality.

BURSEVI:v1p341/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p341/r9.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v1p341/r9.claim: A hadith says a believer's charity protects its giver from worldly calamities, the trial of the grave, and the punishment of Judgment Day.

BURSEVI:v1p342/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p342/r1.speaker: السعدي
BURSEVI:v1p342/r1.claim: Saʿdī's poem recounts ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz selling his precious gem-set ring during a famine and giving the proceeds to the needy rather than remain comfortable while citizens suffered.

BURSEVI:v1p342/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p342/r2.speaker: السعدي
BURSEVI:v1p342/r2.claim: The poem praises preferring people's comfort over one's own and refusing to keep luxury while the poor are distressed.

BURSEVI:v1p342/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p342/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p342/r3.claim: Deeds depend on intentions; the report that a believer's intention is better than his deed means better than a nonbeliever's deed when the believer intended a good act but another dug the well first.

BURSEVI:v1p342/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p342/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p342/r4.claim: An alternative explanation is that a believer's intention alone is better than action performed without intention; some acts need intention, such as prayer, while recitation and remembrance may not.

BURSEVI:v1p342/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p342/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p342/r5.claim: Ordinary believers spend wealth for Paradise, while the elect spend by purifying their character and heart, hoping for the vision of God on Judgment Day.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32#2/r1.claim: After accounts demonstrating resurrection, the passage turns to spending and its recompense at resurrection; similar spending passages follow the earlier account of those fleeing death and David’s fight with Goliath.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32#2/r2.claim: A single earthly seed producing seven hundred grains signals God’s power to raise the dead from their graves, since both processes involve nourishment and growth.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r1.claim: Spending in God’s cause includes all good works, jihad among them; an alternative restricts the special multiplication to jihad and gives other charity only tenfold.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r10.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r10.claim: God has stored for those who finance military campaigns treasures of mercy beyond human knowledge.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r2.claim: An alternative view says the verse’s seven-hundredfold multiplication applies specifically to spending in jihad, while other spending receives the ordinary tenfold reward.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r3.claim: The comparison needs an implied genitive on one side: either their expenditure is like a grain, or the spenders are like someone sowing one grain.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r4.claim: A grain is generally a staple crop, especially wheat; non-food plant seed is more commonly called ḥabba with kasra.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r5.claim: The seed is the causal occasion of growth, but God is the actual grower; the vivid comparison makes an abstract multiplication visible.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r6.claim: The word sunbula is commonly analyzed with an extra nūn, from asbala meaning that grain formed ears; another analysis treats nūn as root, but the first is better known.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r7.claim: God may multiply this reward beyond sevenfold, as well as to seven hundred; the author favors this unrestricted reading as more beneficial.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r8.claim: The degree of reward varies with the spender’s sincerity and effort and with choosing the best occasion for giving.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r9.speaker: ابن ماجه، وابن أبي حاتم
ALUSI-FULL:v3p32/r9.claim: A report from several Companions traces to the Prophet: each dirham sent to support God’s cause earns seven hundred; personally campaigning and spending earns seven hundred thousand on Judgment Day, then he recited the verse.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r1.claim: The spending includes obligatory and voluntary gifts for every good cause, not only a single form of charity.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r10.claim: The promised return is at least seven hundredfold and may multiply further without limit.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r11.claim: In al-Bazzi's reading from Ibn Kathir, the verb is read yuda'ifu, with the same meaning.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r12.claim: Agricultural experiments are said to yield over two thousand grains from one wheat grain by separating and replanting its shoots.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r13.claim: Life's laws work by multiplication, so spending for people's benefit, God's word, and especially the fighters brings unbounded reward with God.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r14.claim: God's vast mercy is not exhausted by abundant spending, and His knowledge accurately encompasses each donor's intention, amount, and promised return.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r15.claim: Sebilullah means God's path or religion; in legal usage it is more commonly associated with jihad because jihad protects religion and believers from coercion.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r16.claim: Some exegetes restrict this verse to fighters who spend their own wealth and the next verse to those who fund other fighters, assigning jihad at least seven hundred against ten for other good deeds.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r17.claim: The preferred view treats ten as the minimum for all good deeds and this verse as general encouragement to spend in every good cause; the next verse explains acceptance conditions.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r18.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r18.claim: Ibn Umar reports that after this verse was revealed, the Prophet prayed for a greater reward for his community, after which 39:10 was revealed.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r2.claim: The seed's seven ears, each with a hundred grains, picture a seven-hundredfold return; believers should not dismiss even one grain or fear spending it.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r3.claim: Divine wisdom makes a seed sprout and multiply; without that order it would rot, so human deeds too can multiply through God's wisdom.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r4.claim: Spending in God's path will take increasingly multiplied forms in the afterlife and be placed on the balance.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r5.claim: The author's example extends the seed's multiplication to human action: a single grain can produce hundreds through God's wisdom.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r6.claim: Because habba can mean any seed, some crops visibly demonstrate the parable's increase, though comparable wheat yields are said to be rare.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r7.claim: Even if such a yield is rare, the verse indicates that divine wisdom permits it at minimum; inadequate cultivation explains why it is not achieved.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r8.claim: Improved agriculture and removal of corruption could attain such yields, ending disputes and despair about insufficient earthly provisions.

ELMALILI:2:261-264/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264/r9.claim: The intended lesson is to spend the crop for God's path, not to accumulate grain; its true harvest comes in Paradise.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r1.claim: The reward and blessing of spending are compared to a seed yielding seven ears of a hundred grains each; fertile soil and rain are omitted because they are implicit, making an intelligible reward visible through a familiar scene.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r2.claim: The seed is the basis of the image because its increase comes from within; beneficence is commonly likened to planting, as the proverb says that a planter may not harvest.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r3.claim: The single baseline for multiplication is the reward for even the least good deed, such as intending a good deed without doing it; spending in God's path earns seven hundredfold.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r4.speaker: الواحدي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r4.claim: Al-Wāḥidī and others report that the verse concerned ʿUthmān and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, who equipped the army of hardship before Tabūk with substantial donations.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p41#2/r5.claim: God's multiplication has many degrees known only to Him, varying with donor, recipient, time, place, sincerity, obedience, goodwill, and self-sacrifice.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r1.speaker: علي عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r1.claim: Ali laments that good is receding, evil increasing, Satan's power growing, the rich deny God's favor, the miser withholds God's due, and the defiant turn deaf to counsel.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r2.claim: Al-Tabataba'i argues that modern Western materialism concentrates wealth and pleasures among the powerful, deprives most people, fuels vice and class conflict, and threatens social peace and human life.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r3.claim: He identifies blocked giving and expanding usury as major causes of social corruption, saying the later seven verses on usury disclose harms already latent at the Qur'an's revelation.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#2/r4.claim: He asks readers to consider the connected discussion in Surah al-Rum on innate religion, giving, usury, and corruption caused by human deeds.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r1.claim: The multiplication language recalls 2:245, where abundance is left unbounded rather than tied to a number.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r2.speaker: قيل
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r2.claim: An alternative reading says God multiplies this multiplication for whomever He wills, with seven hundred as the verse's stated ceiling.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r3.claim: If the clause meant that multiplication is the cause, it should begin with inna; the grammar weighs against that restricted reading.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r4.claim: The parable is not restricted to the afterlife; its unrestricted wording and ordinary social consequences encompass this life as well.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r5.claim: Human society functions like one body: when a member loses health, all members' work and common purposes suffer.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r6.claim: Giving resources to repair another member's deprivation restores the whole and returns benefits to the donor many times over, including love, good memory, and energy.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r7.claim: Spending on shared needs such as education and upbringing especially produces this social return.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#3/r8.claim: Repairing a deficient member with resources saved from another restores the condition of the whole community.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r1.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r1.claim: Al-Bāqir says believers and Muslims have equal standing in inheritance and rulings under the Imam, while believers have an advantage in the deeds they perform.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r2.claim: In response to the question about shared prayer, al-Bāqir says believers' good deeds are multiplied seventyfold and further according to the soundness of faith, by God's will.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r3.claim: The author says related reports rightly read God's multiplication generally, not as restricted to spenders by the occasion; each good-doer may receive seven hundred, more, or less in proportion to goodness.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r4.claim: The report's wording combines the multiplication clause in 2:261 with 2:245 by meaning; this does not conflict with rejecting the specific restriction to spenders.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#6/r5.claim: The narration also indicates that deeds by nonbelievers from other Muslim groups can be accepted and rewarded; the commentary returns to this at 4:98.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r1.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r1.claim: Al-Majmaʿ reports from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq that the verse applies generally to spending, including jihad and other forms of good works.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r2.claim: A report through Ayyub says the Prophet rejected the idea that only a fighter is in God's path: earning lawful support for parents, family, or oneself is also in God's path, while seeking mere accumulation follows Satan.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r4.claim: Reports from both traditions establish that every act God approves is in His path and every expenditure in His path is charity.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.claim: The connected themes suggest this passage was revealed as one unit: spending grows seven hundredfold or more, sincere giving bears fruit, ostentation and reminders or harm ruin reward, good wealth should be given, the poor detained in God's path are recipients, and the reward is great.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.claim: The passage orders its teaching around purpose (giving for God, not people), manner (without reproach or injury), quality (good rather than bad wealth), recipient (the needy constrained in God's path), and reward.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r3.speaker: author
