TABATABAI:2:261-274/r3.claim: Islam makes material rights a major concern through obligatory and recommended transfers, including zakat, khums, expiations, charity, endowments, gifts, and bequests.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r4.claim: Financial giving is meant to raise the living standard of the poor while restraining ostentatious excess among the wealthy, producing a moderate, mutually supportive social life and reducing envy and hostility.

TABATABAI:2:261/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261/r1.claim: God's way means any religious purpose or act intended to attain His satisfaction; the phrase is general, and earlier battle context or common association with jihad does not restrict it.

TABATABAI:2:261/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261/r2.speaker: بعض المفسرين
TABATABAI:2:261/r2.claim: Some exegetes parse the parable as “like one who planted a grain,” so the multiplying grain represents the spender's wealth rather than the spender.

TABATABAI:2:261/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261/r3.claim: Although that parsing seems reasonable, Qur'anic parables often name only the central image; here the grain and its yield are the core likeness, with the planter supplied to complete the story.

TABATABAI:2:264/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:264/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:264/r1.claim: The author illustrates how a parable can prompt listeners to recall and apply a familiar story, such as the saying “No she-camel or camel.”

TABATABAI:2:264/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:264/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:264/r2.claim: Some Qur'anic comparisons target the whole story, while in the spending parable only the seed yielding seven hundred is essential and the planter completes the imagined scenario; abbreviation leaves the listener to supply what is omitted.

TABATABAI:2:264/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:264/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:264/r3.claim: Sunbul is a known term on the faʿnal pattern, said to derive from covering because the ear encloses its grains; the objection that one ear cannot contain one hundred grains fails because parables may be hypothetical and such yields are possible.

TABATABAI:2:264/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:264/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:264/r4.claim: God's multiplication means more than seven hundred for whoever He wills; His generosity is unlimited and He knows whom to favor.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r1.claim: The following fourteen verses treat spending and charity without changing subject; the wisdom in verse 269 means preferring generosity and aid over miserliness and selfishness.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r10.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r10.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r10.claim: Islamic social economics aims to provide everyone with ordinary needs whether or not they work; people first seek to meet needs through labor, and those with excess help people who cannot work or whose income is insufficient.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r11.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r11.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r11.claim: Aid takes forms including maintenance, charity, zakat, fitr charity, sacrifice, gifts, lending for use, endowments, continuing charity, and state subsistence payments.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r12.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r12.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r12.claim: A third rule is to forbid waste: the wealthy should avoid ostentation in housing, transport, food, clothing, and recreation and remember that wealth is a test and its blessings will be accounted for.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r13.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r13.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r13.claim: Even when performing ablution from a river, a believer must use only enough water.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r14.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r14.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r14.claim: A fourth rule forbids interest; persistent usury blocks social justice and welfare, and implementing Islam's principles would remove debilitating poverty and bring greater peace.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r15.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r15.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r15.claim: Any spending in obedience and worship that helps Islam or Muslims is in God's path; the most virtuous is spending for jihad to strengthen, protect, and defend Islam.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r16.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r16.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r16.claim: Spending in God's path earns a seven-hundredfold return, compared with the usual tenfold reward for good deeds, both encouraging giving and reflecting its greater difficulty because people tend toward miserliness.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r2.claim: Infak means consuming or spending; nafaka shares its root, while sadaqa includes money, goods, services, and material or spiritual help given as worship for God's pleasure.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r3.claim: The surrounding verses teach that charitable spending should seek God's pleasure rather than human praise.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r4.claim: Charitable giving should not be followed by reminders of the gift or by hurtful treatment.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r5.claim: Charity should be given from good rather than poor-quality property.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r6.claim: Priority should go to people unable to earn because of legitimate duties or other impediments.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r7.claim: Spending brings major benefits in worldly life and the hereafter.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r8.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r8.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r8.claim: Human beings cannot sustain themselves alone, and differences in people's capacities make organized arrangements necessary for shared wellbeing.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r9.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r9.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:261/r9.claim: Surplus divinely given wealth should be transferred to those in need; otherwise disparities generate demands, anger, hostility, coercion, and conflict, as historical and political experience shows.

QIRAAT-ER:2:261:17#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:261:17#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:261:17#1/r1.claim: Hamzah is removed in miyatu, a dialectal pronunciation with no semantic change.

QIRAAT-ER:2:261:21#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:2:261:21#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:2:261:21#1/r1.claim: Form II expresses simple doubling, while Form III suggests intensive multiplication; both readings are canonical.

STUDYQURAN:2:261/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:261/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:261/r1.claim: The promise that God multiplies reward echoes the Quranic promise to reward the best deeds and increase from divine bounty.

STUDYQURAN:2:261/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:261/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:261/r2.claim: Al-Wāsiʿ, the All-Encompassing, also means generous.

STUDYQURAN:2:261/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:261/r3.speaker: Prophet
STUDYQURAN:2:261/r3.claim: A prophetic report says good deeds may be multiplied tenfold or seven hundredfold, while fasting is reserved for God’s own reward.

STUDYQURAN:2:261/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:261/r4.speaker: Prophet
STUDYQURAN:2:261/r4.claim: A man who offered a camel in God’s way was told he would receive seven hundred camels on Judgment Day.
